title: Money and business
summary: The vocabulary of earning, owing and trading.

questions.clue: This is the long-term loan taken out to buy a house, with the house itself as security.
questions.note: The t is silent. From Old French words meaning dead pledge, because the arrangement dies when the debt is paid.

questions.clue: This is the general rise in prices over time, which makes money buy less than it did.
questions.note: The opposite is deflation. Prices rising more slowly than before is disinflation, which is not the same as falling.

questions.clue: This is the document a business sends listing what is owed and asking to be paid.
questions.note: A receipt is the opposite: proof that payment has already been made.

questions.clue: This word describes a person or company officially declared unable to pay their debts.
questions.note: Insolvent describes the financial state; bankrupt is the legal status that follows a court process.

questions.clue: This is the plan setting out how much money is available and what it will be spent on.
questions.note: From a word for a small leather bag, which is what a chancellor once carried the accounts in.

questions.clue: This is the share of a company's profit paid out to the people who own its shares.
questions.note: Profit kept in the business rather than paid out is called retained earnings.

questions.clue: This is a period of several months during which a country's economy shrinks rather than grows.
questions.note: The common working definition is two consecutive quarters of falling output. A very deep and long one is a depression.

questions.clue: This word describes selling goods in large quantities to shops rather than to the public.
questions.note: Selling to the public is retail. Wholesale also means on a large scale, as in wholesale changes.

questions.clue: This is the sum paid up front as part of a larger price, or left as security on a rented flat.
questions.note: The same word means money put into a bank account, and the material left behind by a river.

questions.clue: This is money given back to you when you return goods or were charged too much.
questions.note: A reimbursement pays back what you spent on somebody else's behalf; a rebate returns part of a price already paid.
